parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a member of the platform's airspace desk. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you finish?
I don't know.
What is the very first thing you do when you sit down at your desk to start a shift?
I don't know.
What kind of tasks come across your desk during a shift?

My work on the airspace desk involves keeping the shared picture of the airspace up to date. This means maintaining the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
Could you give me a concrete example of what you look for to see how much disruption a closure caused across customers?
I don't know.
How do closures announced by the authorities get to you, and who hands that information over?
I don't know.
Once you update a corridor, zone, or closure, who do you pass that work on to, or who uses it next?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the desk, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong in the airspace or with a closure, what do you need to know right away?
I don't know.
What parts of the airspace picture do you currently double-check by hand because you don't fully trust them?
I don't know.
When you think about a new software service being built for your desk, what are you most afraid it would get wrong?
I worry about updates and restarts happening during working hours while drones are flying, as well as occasional crashes, even though the companies accept a few minutes of interruption.
What happens on your desk right after a crash or interruption occurs while drones are flying?
I don't know.
Can you tell me more about how you maintain the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace by maintaining the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
What information about the individual customer companies can you see—or not see—when you work with sites and disruption?
I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business.
If each company's sites and jobs are private, how are the flight corridors between sites set up, and how is disruption across customers measured?
I don't know.
How many closures, corridors, or zones are you typically dealing with at one time?
I don't know.
